name: Ebony
lede: Ebony is the name of a dense tropical heartwood and, from it, of a glossy black; the swatch on screen is a dark green-grey, which is a good reason to read what the books say about the wood.

sections.title: A wood that became a color
sections.body:
Ebony is the heartwood of tropical trees of the genus *Diospyros*, and the color is named from it [2]. Paterson's dictionary defines the color as black, taken from the wood, and cites Shakespeare's phrase "ebon-coloured ink" in *Love's Labour's Lost* [1]. St Clair's glossary gives something different: a very dark brown [2]. The books disagree, and the disagreement is the interesting part, because the wood sits right on the line between the two.

Paterson also files ebony among the wood colors, beside mahogany, oak, pine, teak and walnut [3]. In English the comparison with ebony is one of the stock similes for blackness, listed with death, hell, ink, jet, night, pitch and soot [4]. The Pigment Compendium, which catalogues pigment names, labels the entry *Ebony* as black-brown [5]. Three sources, and three slightly different darks.

sections.title: The swatch is not black
sections.body:
The swatch here, #555D50, is a dark grey with a clear green cast, at a lightness of about 38 out of 100 [6]. It comes from the old charts: Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary records the name as first used in 1596, and Ridgway's 1912 plate XLVI and the ISCC-NBS 1955 system (block 108) also carry it [6]. The library's nearest equivalent is Dark Greyish Olive, a mere 1.5 units away, and the nearest app color is [[hunter-green]], 12.6 units away [6].

Neither book describes the wood as olive, so the chart is giving an idea of an ebony-colored object rather than the heartwood itself [1][2]. If you want the color the word usually means, think of [[black]] with a trace of brown. The swatch is closer to [[green-grey]] than to [[jet]].

sections.title: Black in myth and in argument
sections.body:
Ebony is old as a word for black. Pastoureau's history of black places Hades, god of the Greek underworld, on an ebony throne, in the palace at the center of the dark world below [7]. In late antiquity Boethius used ebony to make a philosophical point: the one word *black* is applied to a person, to a crow and to ebony, so color is an accident and tells us nothing about the nature of a thing [8].

Be careful reading too much into such words. Pastoureau notes that the Hebrew Bible is rich in terms for materials such as gold, ivory and ebony and poor in terms for color, and that material and color are often confused [9]. A passage that mentions ebony may mean the wood, the color, or both.

sections.title: Ebony as a pigment name
sections.body:
Ebony black turns up as a pigment name in nineteenth-century sources, but not as a black made from the wood. The Pigment Compendium reports that Riffault and colleagues, in 1874, describe ebony black as obtained by burning copper nitrate with peat [5]. The resulting composition is unknown [5]. The same entry notes that Field stated in 1835 that olive lake was prepared from ebony, though by the end of the century olive lake was a blend of other pigments, among them quercitron lake, bone brown and ultramarine [5][10].

So the name outlived any clear recipe. When an old color box says *ebony*, the safe reading is a dark, glossy tone, and nothing more specific can be claimed.

sections.title: Where to look
sections.body: The books use ebony for gloss more than for hue. Finlay describes amber ranging from ivory to ebony, with all the other colors in between [11]. Jarman puts ebony on a silk dress and a desk [12]. Finlay's Suffolk sheep, in the same spirit, have ebony faces [13]. Hold a black wooden object in daylight and see whether it leans brown or stays neutral: the two glosses in the dictionaries, black and very dark brown, are about exactly that lean.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 1,344 works, 5.7 per cent [14]. It is mostly a mid-tone, playing that role in 58 per cent of the paintings that carry it, against 30 per cent as a shadow [14]. The largest examples are quiet: Købke's *Study of Clouds over the Sea* of 1840, at 86 per cent of the canvas, and [[painter:james-mcneill-whistler|Whistler's]] [[painting:aic-56905|Nocturne: Blue and Gold, Southampton Water]] of 1872, at 75 per cent [14].

It has grown more common with time. The 1900s carry it in 172 of 1,674 works, 10.3 per cent, a lift of 1.8 over the archive rate, and the 1930s peak at 9 of 69 [14]. It is most at home in Tibetan paintings (9 of 47), Norwegian paintings (19 of 120) and Post-Impressionism (8 of 45) [14]. The Danish painter [[painter:harald-giersing|Giersing]] has it in 8 of his 23 works [14]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [14].
